doc.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Parents' attitudes to a music career and the Northwestern math scholarship
summary: His mother opposed music, his father left it to him, and he nearly became a computer programmer after a math scholarship to Northwestern.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did your father feel that music was a good profession for his son?
Did you get that impression, or did he kind of just let you—

I’ll tell you, my mother, you asked me about my father but I’m going to tell you about my mother and say she would say no. Clearly. She didn’t want me to do that. My father didn’t say yes or no. He decided if it was in me, that’s the way it would be. So I never
really got — he always told me it was difficult, and it is. But he never really tried to influence me. I did it on my own.
Your mother probably would have been happier with a more conventional way of—

She would have. And I came very close to it because I received a four year scholarship for mathematics to Northwestern University. And I attended Northwestern, I graduated from Northwestern University. I went to get a master’s degree at Governor’s State but by that time I got my master’s degree in music. But prior to that I was going to be some kind of mathematician or, actually I got involved in computer science. And I almost went that direction. Because I became a computer programmer. I programmed in like Fortran, ALGOL and COBOL back in the — that’s the early languages of computers. And I thought about it, but then I switched over to music. She wasn’t too happy about that. But she wasn’t—
